title: Cloning could be used to save species—or make human “organ sacks”
gist: A Checkup newsletter survey of cloning's use cases, pegged to Ishiuchi and Matoba's CRISPR method for cutting the Y chromosome to make female clones of male mice. It walks the value chain from Dolly (1996) through commercial pet cloning at tens of thousands of dollars, frozen-zoo biobanks like San Diego Zoo's 1,300-plus species collection, de-extinction efforts at Colossal Biosciences, and a startup founder's pitch for brainless human clones grown as replacement organs.

insights.claim: Researchers have developed a CRISPR-based approach that cuts out the Y chromosome to create female mouse clones genetically identical to a male donor except for the missing Y.
insights.speaker: Jessica Hamzelou
insights.so_what: Removes the sex constraint on cloning, which is the specific reason cloned recovery programs stall when only male genetic material survives.
insights.quote: That’s right: female animals that are genetically identical to males, except for the missing Y chromosome.
insights.locator: This week I spoke to scientists

insights.claim: Ishiuchi and Matoba's stated target application is conservation, specifically cases where only a few individuals of a species remain.
insights.speaker: Jessica Hamzelou
insights.so_what: Conservation framing shapes which funders and regulators engage first, even where the near-term commercial value sits elsewhere.
insights.locator: Ishiuchi and his colleague Shogo Matoba

insights.claim: The Dolly method — transferring an adult cell's nucleus into an enucleated egg and implanting the resulting embryo in a surrogate — has been the working template for mammalian cloning since 1996.
insights.speaker: Jessica Hamzelou
insights.so_what: Thirty years on, the core process is unchanged; innovation is happening in chromosome editing and inputs, not the transfer step itself.
insights.locator: We can’t talk about cloning without mentioning Dolly

insights.claim: The original commercial motivation behind Dolly was genetically modifying livestock, with cloning offering a faster path than the selective breeding farmers have used for thousands of years to fix desirable traits.
insights.speaker: Jessica Hamzelou
insights.so_what: Agriculture, not medicine, was the original economic driver — worth remembering when handicapping which cloning applications actually scale.
insights.locator: The scientists behind that work were interested

insights.claim: Commercial pet cloning is an active market at a price somewhere in the tens of thousands of dollars, with clients including Barbra Streisand and Tom Brady.
insights.speaker: Jessica Hamzelou
insights.so_what: A real revenue-generating consumer price point for cloning today — the benchmark against which conservation or medical applications must justify their costs.
insights.locator: Cloning is also being used to replicate deceased pets

insights.claim: Pet cloning carries an ethical drag because it requires donor egg cells and a surrogate animal with no medical or environmental justification, which bioethicist Jessica Pierce calls the exploitation of the canine underclass.
insights.speaker: Jessica Hamzelou
insights.so_what: Animal-welfare framing is the plausible vector for restrictions on consumer cloning — a regulatory risk distinct from human-cloning bans.
insights.quote: One bioethicist, Jessica Pierce, has described this aspect of dog cloning as “the exploitation of the canine underclass.”
insights.locator: Considering that cloning also requires egg cells

insights.claim: The San Diego Zoo's frozen zoo currently holds cryopreserved cells from over 1,300 species, some collected decades ago, making it a stock of irreplaceable genetic material rather than a research curiosity.
insights.speaker: Jessica Hamzelou
insights.so_what: A concrete, sized biobank asset whose value rises with every advance in cloning and chromosome editing.
insights.locator: Some of these tissues are cryopreserved

insights.claim: Preserved tissue has already enabled cloning of species near extinction including black-footed ferrets and Przewalski’s horse, establishing that biobank-to-live-animal is a working pipeline, not a concept.
insights.speaker: Jessica Hamzelou
insights.so_what: Proof the cryo-to-clone pathway works reduces technical risk for anyone funding biobank expansion.
insights.locator: Preserved tissues like these have enabled scientists

insights.claim: The 2009 Pyrenean ibex de-extinction attempt in Spain required 439 embryos created from decade-old cryopreserved skin cells using domestic goat eggs, yielded a single live birth, and that female died minutes later from a lung defect.
insights.speaker: Jessica Hamzelou
insights.so_what: A 439-to-zero effective success rate is the hard efficiency baseline any de-extinction business case has to beat.
insights.quote: It’s the only animal we know of that has gone extinct twice.

insights.claim: Colossal Biosciences aims to revive long-extinct species such as the thylacine and woolly mammoth, but its efforts so far have largely involved modifying the genomes of modern-day animals rather than true cloning from ancient material.
insights.speaker: Jessica Hamzelou
insights.so_what: A gap between de-extinction marketing and the actual technical method — the diligence question for anyone underwriting that company's claims.
insights.quote: So far, the company’s efforts have largely involved modifying the genomes of modern-day animals.

insights.claim: Human cloning is technically possible with existing methods and no known instance has occurred, meaning the barrier is regulatory and ethical rather than technical.
insights.speaker: Jessica Hamzelou
insights.so_what: Where the constraint is norms rather than capability, the risk of a fast unilateral move by one actor is materially higher.
insights.quote: Technically, it’s also possible to clone humans. As far as we know, no one has done it.
insights.locator: Technically, it’s also possible to clone humans

insights.claim: A biotech startup founder has pitched brainless human clones — clones lacking a brain but containing a full set of transplantable organs — as a future source of replacement organs, a pitch Antonio Regalado documented in March.
insights.speaker: Jessica Hamzelou
insights.so_what: Signals venture-side appetite for extreme organ-supply solutions; watch which investors touch it, since regulatory blowback would be category-wide.
insights.quote: One biotech startup founder has pitched an idea for “brainless clones”—human clones that lack a brain but contain all the organs people might need to replace their own in future.
insights.locator: But some have played with the idea

insights.claim: The author's own posture toward cloning's trajectory is explicitly ambivalent — excited but slightly nervous about the coming decades — reflecting that even sympathetic science press is not underwriting the field's direction.
insights.speaker: Jessica Hamzelou
insights.so_what: Ambivalence in friendly coverage is an early indicator of the reputational headwind commercial cloning ventures will face.
insights.quote: I’m excited—but also slightly nervous—about what the coming decades will bring.
insights.locator: Scientists have done a hell of a lot with cloning
